short: Constantine refounded the Greek city of Byzantium as a new imperial capital on the Bosphorus.
full:
Constantine consecrated the site of a new capital at the old Greek colony of Byzantium on 8 November 324 CE, shortly after defeating his last rival, Licinius, at nearby Chrysopolis. Building proceeded at pace on a peninsula chosen for its defensible position between the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara, and the city was formally dedicated on 11 May 330, marked by forty days of games and ceremony. Constantine styled it Nova Roma, New Rome, complete with its own forum, senate house, hippodrome and imperial palace, though it soon took his own name instead.

The new city drew on the resources and, in places, the monuments of older cities across the empire to furnish it quickly, and Constantine attracted settlers with grants of land and a free grain distribution modelled on Rome's. Within decades it had eclipsed Rome as the empire's effective political centre, and after the western empire's collapse in 476 it remained the capital of what continued, uninterrupted, as the Roman state for another thousand years.
